subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department smelling of alcohol. He is emotionally labile, speaks with slurred words, and is ataxic. Laboratory studies show an AST value approximately twice the ALT value. His vital signs are stable and he is treated with fluids and antiemetics.
question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this patient's intoxication and associated laboratory finding?

options.text: Positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors with inhibition of NMDA-mediated excitation; AST is roughly twice ALT
Reversal of VMAT and DAT with increased monoamine release; AST is roughly twice ALT
Antagonism of NMDA receptors without GABA-A involvement; AST is roughly twice ALT
Blockade of dopamine reuptake at DAT; AST is roughly twice ALT
Antagonism of adenosine receptors; AST is roughly twice ALT

explanation_correct: Alcohol is a GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator and also inhibits glutamate-induced excitation of NMDA receptors, producing sedation, emotional lability, slurred speech, ataxia, coma, and blackouts. Chronic use elevates AST to about twice the ALT value ('ToAST 2 ALcohol'). Treatment of intoxication is supportive with fluids and antiemetics. The increased GABAergic and decreased glutamatergic tone accounts for the depressant effects.

explanation_incorrect.B: Reversal of VMAT and DAT describes amphetamines, not alcohol, and would produce mydriasis, wakefulness, and hypertension rather than sedation and ataxia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Although alcohol does inhibit NMDA-mediated excitation, it is also a GABA-A positive allosteric modulator; pure NMDA antagonism without GABA effects is characteristic of PCP.
explanation_incorrect.D: Blockade of dopamine reuptake at DAT describes cocaine, which causes stimulation, paranoia, and formication rather than slurred speech and ataxia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Adenosine receptor antagonism is the mechanism of caffeine, which causes palpitations, agitation, and insomnia, not alcohol intoxication.

educationalObjective: Alcohol intoxication reflects GABA-A positive allosteric modulation and NMDA inhibition with slurred speech and ataxia, and an AST:ALT ratio of about 2:1.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 55-year-old man with alcohol use disorder stops drinking abruptly. About 8 hours later he has tremors, insomnia, diaphoresis, and agitation. At 10 hours he has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. His wife reports that on a prior withdrawal he saw 'bugs on the walls' roughly a day and a half after his last drink, followed by a severe confused state with fever and hallucinations on the third day.
question: Which of the following correctly matches these withdrawal phenomena to their typical timing?

options.text: Delirium tremens occurs 6-12 hours after the last drink; withdrawal seizures occur 48-96 hours
Withdrawal seizures occur 48-96 hours after the last drink; alcoholic hallucinosis is usually auditory
Tremors and insomnia first appear 24-36 hours after the last drink; hallucinosis occurs at 6-12 hours
Tremors, insomnia, and diaphoresis occur early (around 3 hours), withdrawal seizures at 6-12 hours, hallucinosis at 24-36 hours, and delirium tremens at 48-96 hours
Alcoholic hallucinosis occurs 6-12 hours after the last drink and is usually visual, with delirium tremens at 24-36 hours

explanation_correct: Alcohol withdrawal results from adaptation with increased glutamate receptors, producing unregulated excess excitation when alcohol is removed. The timeline is: tremors, insomnia, diaphoresis, agitation, and GI upset at about 3 hours; withdrawal seizures at 6-12 hours; alcoholic hallucinosis (usually visual) at 24-36 hours; and delirium tremens at 48-96 hours. This patient's early tremors and 10-hour seizure fit the early part of this sequence, and his prior visual hallucinosis and third-day confusion fit the later stages.

explanation_incorrect.A: The timing is reversed; delirium tremens occurs at 48-96 hours and withdrawal seizures at 6-12 hours after the last drink.
explanation_incorrect.B: Withdrawal seizures occur at 6-12 hours rather than 48-96 hours, and alcoholic hallucinosis is usually visual, not auditory.
explanation_incorrect.C: Tremors and insomnia appear early (around 3 hours), not at 24-36 hours, while hallucinosis occurs at 24-36 hours rather than 6-12 hours.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hallucinosis occurs at 24-36 hours and delirium tremens at 48-96 hours; the times given are too early for both.

educationalObjective: Alcohol withdrawal follows a timeline of early tremors/insomnia (about 3 hours), seizures (6-12 hours), visual hallucinosis (24-36 hours), and delirium tremens (48-96 hours).

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 33-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after ingesting a large amount of a prescribed sedative. He has marked respiratory depression, hypotension, delirium, and progressing cardiovascular collapse. The drug is known to have a low safety margin. Treatment focuses on assisted respiration and blood pressure support.
question: Which class of drug is most consistent with this presentation and mechanism?

options.text: Adenosine receptor antagonists, which cause palpitations and insomnia
5-HT2A receptor agonists, which cause hallucinations and flashbacks
GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulators with a low safety margin and marked respiratory depression
Opioid receptor agonists, which produce miosis and decreased GI motility
NMDA receptor antagonists, which cause violence and nystagmus

explanation_correct: Barbiturates are GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulators with a low safety margin, so overdose produces marked respiratory depression, delirium, and life-threatening cardiovascular collapse. Management is symptom-based, including assistance with respiration and blood pressure support. This contrasts with benzodiazepines, which act at the same receptor but have a much wider safety margin and cause only minor respiratory depression.

explanation_incorrect.A: Adenosine receptor antagonists such as caffeine are stimulants causing palpitations, agitation, tremor, and insomnia, not respiratory depression and collapse.
explanation_incorrect.B: 5-HT2A agonists such as LSD cause perceptual distortion and flashbacks, not the profound respiratory and cardiovascular depression described.
explanation_incorrect.D: Opioid receptor agonists cause miosis, decreased GI motility, and respiratory depression, but the low safety margin with delirium and cardiovascular collapse is characteristic of barbiturates.
explanation_incorrect.E: NMDA antagonists such as PCP cause violence, nystagmus, impulsivity, and analgesia rather than a depressant overdose with cardiovascular collapse.

educationalObjective: Barbiturates are GABA-A positive allosteric modulators with a low safety margin, causing marked respiratory depression, delirium, and cardiovascular collapse in overdose.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 40-year-old man takes an excessive dose of alprazolam and is found to be ataxic but breathing adequately. His physician mentions that this class has a wide safety margin and that an antagonist is available for overdose. The patient has also used the drug chronically and is at risk for seizures and depression if he stops suddenly.
question: Which of the following statements about this drug class is correct?

options.text: It has a low safety margin, and flumazenil is contraindicated in overdose
It acts by reversing monoamine transporters and is treated with cyproheptadine
It is an NMDA receptor antagonist whose withdrawal causes flashbacks
It is an opioid receptor agonist whose overdose is treated with naloxone
It acts as a GABA-A positive allosteric modulator with a wide safety margin; flumazenil is the antagonist and withdrawal can cause seizures and depression

explanation_correct: Benzodiazepines are GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulators with a greater safety margin than barbiturates. Intoxication causes ataxia and only minor respiratory depression; flumazenil is a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist used in overdose. Chronic use followed by discontinuation can cause withdrawal with seizures, sleep disturbance, and depression. These features distinguish benzodiazepines from the lower-safety-margin barbiturates.

explanation_incorrect.A: Benzodiazepines have a wide, not low, safety margin, and flumazenil is indeed the receptor antagonist used in overdose.
explanation_incorrect.B: Reversal of monoamine transporters is the mechanism of amphetamines; cyproheptadine is a 5-HT2 antagonist for serotonin syndrome, not benzodiazepine overdose.
explanation_incorrect.C: NMDA antagonism is the mechanism of PCP, and flashbacks are associated with LSD, not benzodiazepines.
explanation_incorrect.D: Opioid receptor agonism with naloxone reversal describes opioids, which cause miosis and decreased GI motility rather than ataxia with a wide safety margin.

educationalObjective: Benzodiazepines are GABA-A positive allosteric modulators with a wide safety margin; flumazenil reverses overdose and withdrawal can cause seizures, sleep disturbance, and depression.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 28-year-old man is found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and slowed breathing. He has decreased bowel sounds and a depressed gag reflex. He is the most common cause of drug overdose death in the United States, and he is given an antagonist that rapidly reverses his respiratory depression.
question: Which of the following best describes the drug's mechanism and the reversal agent?

options.text: CB1 receptor agonism with conjunctival injection; reversal with cyproheptadine
Opioid receptor activation causing miosis, decreased GI motility, respiratory/CNS depression, euphoria, and reduced gag reflex; reversal with naloxone
GABA-A modulation causing ataxia; reversal with flumazenil
Dopamine reuptake blockade causing paranoia; reversal with haloperidol
Adenosine antagonism causing palpitations; reversal with caffeine

explanation_correct: Opioids act at opioid receptors, and activation of mu receptors causes the prototypic miosis (pinpoint pupils), decreased GI motility, respiratory and CNS depression, euphoria, a reduced gag reflex, and seizures. Opioids are the most common cause of drug overdose death. The overdose treatment is naloxone, an opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses respiratory depression. The pinpoint pupils and depressed gag reflex are classic clues.

explanation_incorrect.A: CB1 agonism from cannabis causes euphoria, increased appetite, dry mouth, and conjunctival injection with dilated, not pinpoint, pupils; cyproheptadine is not a reversal agent.
explanation_incorrect.C: GABA-A modulation from benzodiazepines causes ataxia and minor respiratory depression with normal or mildly affected pupils; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.
explanation_incorrect.D: Dopamine reuptake blockade from cocaine causes mydriasis, paranoia, and formication, not pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression; haloperidol is not an overdose antidote.
explanation_incorrect.E: Adenosine antagonism from caffeine causes palpitations, agitation, tremor, and insomnia, not CNS and respiratory depression with miosis.

educationalObjective: Opioid intoxication causes miosis, decreased GI motility, respiratory/CNS depression, euphoria, and a depressed gag reflex; naloxone reverses overdose.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 35-year-old woman with a history of daily heroin use is incarcerated and abruptly stops using the drug. After about a day she develops dilated pupils, diarrhea, rhinorrhea, yawning, nausea, sweating, lacrimation, piloerection, and muscle aches described as flu-like. She is otherwise alert and in no respiratory distress.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this syndrome and its treatment?

options.text: Opioid intoxication with pinpoint pupils and constipation; treat with naloxone
Benzodiazepine withdrawal with ataxia and slurred speech; treat with flumazenil
Opioid withdrawal with mydriasis, diarrhea, flu-like symptoms, rhinorrhea, yawning, nausea, sweating, and piloerection; treat with methadone or buprenorphine
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome with rigidity and fever; treat with dantrolene
Inhalant intoxication with euphoria and a perioral rash; treat supportively

explanation_correct: Opioid withdrawal produces mydriasis, diarrhea, flu-like symptoms, rhinorrhea, yawning, nausea, sweating, piloerection (the 'cold turkey' appearance), and lacrimation. It is the opposite of the intoxication picture of miosis and decreased GI motility. Treatment is symptomatic management along with methadone or buprenorphine, which are opioid agonist/maintenance therapies. The dilated pupils, diarrhea, and piloerection are classic clues.

explanation_incorrect.A: Intoxication causes pinpoint pupils, constipation, and respiratory depression, not the dilated pupils, diarrhea, and piloerection of withdrawal; naloxone would worsen withdrawal.
explanation_incorrect.B: Benzodiazepine withdrawal features seizures, sleep disturbance, and depression, not rhinorrhea, yawning, and piloerection; flumazenil is used for overdose, not withdrawal.
explanation_incorrect.D: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome has fever, lead-pipe rigidity, and elevated CK from antipsychotics, not the flu-like autonomic symptoms of opioid withdrawal.
explanation_incorrect.E: Inhalants cause rapid-onset disinhibition, euphoria, slurred speech, ataxia, and a perioral rash, not this withdrawal syndrome after opioid cessation.

educationalObjective: Opioid withdrawal causes mydriasis, diarrhea, flu-like symptoms, rhinorrhea, yawning, sweating, and piloerection and is treated with symptom management plus methadone or buprenorphine.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by friends after 'huffing' paint thinner. He has rapid-onset disinhibition, euphoria, slurred speech, ataxia, disorientation, and drowsiness. A perioral rash is noted. His symptoms resolve almost completely within an hour, leaving him irritable with a headache.
question: Which of the following best explains this drug's mechanism and the nature of its effects?

options.text: NMDA receptor antagonism causing violence and nystagmus with a prolonged duration
5-HT2A receptor agonism causing perceptual distortion and flashbacks
Opioid receptor agonism causing miosis and decreased GI motility
Enhanced GABA signaling causing disinhibition and ataxia with rapid onset and resolution
Adenosine receptor antagonism causing palpitations and tremor

explanation_correct: Inhalants enhance GABA signaling and produce disinhibition, euphoria, slurred speech, ataxia, disorientation, drowsiness, and a characteristic periorifical rash. Their effects have a rapid onset and rapid resolution, distinguishing them from most other depressants. Withdrawal or after-effects can include irritability, dysphoria, sleep disturbance, and headache. The perioral rash and very short duration are key clues.

explanation_incorrect.A: NMDA antagonism with violence, nystagmus, impulsivity, and analgesia describes PCP, which does not produce the rapid resolution and perioral rash of inhalants.
explanation_incorrect.B: 5-HT2A agonism from LSD causes visual and auditory perceptual distortion, depersonalization, and flashbacks, not a perioral rash with rapid resolution.
explanation_incorrect.C: Opioid receptor agonism causes miosis, decreased GI motility, respiratory depression, and euphoria, not disorientation with a perioral rash and rapid clearance.
explanation_incorrect.E: Adenosine antagonism from caffeine causes palpitations, agitation, tremor, and insomnia rather than disinhibition, ataxia, and a perioral rash.

educationalObjective: Inhalants enhance GABA signaling, causing rapid-onset and rapidly resolving disinhibition, euphoria, slurred speech, ataxia, and a characteristic perioral rash.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 47-year-old man abruptly discontinues a sedative-hypnotic depressant after using it daily for months. One day later he is anxious and tremulous and cannot sleep, and he has a generalized seizure. He has no hallucinations, pupillary changes, or muscle spasms localized to a single group.
question: Which of the following represents the nonspecific withdrawal syndrome seen with depressants?

options.text: Anxiety, tremor, seizures, and insomnia
Mydriasis, diarrhea, and piloerection
Flashbacks and perceptual distortion
Formication and paranoid delusions
Bruxism and hyponatremia

explanation_correct: Nonspecific depressant withdrawal produces anxiety, tremor, seizures, and insomnia, reflecting rebound hyperexcitation after chronic sedative use. This is the general withdrawal pattern described for depressants as a class, which also includes alcohol and benzodiazepines. The seizure in this patient is consistent with the withdrawal seizures seen 6-12 hours after alcohol cessation or with abrupt benzodiazepine discontinuation.

explanation_incorrect.B: Mydriasis, diarrhea, and piloerection are features of opioid withdrawal, not the nonspecific anxiety-tremor-seizure-insomnia pattern of depressant withdrawal.
explanation_incorrect.C: Flashbacks and perceptual distortion are associated with hallucinogens such as LSD, not with depressant withdrawal.
explanation_incorrect.D: Formication and paranoid delusions are stimulant intoxication findings seen with cocaine or amphetamines, not depressant withdrawal.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bruxism and hyponatremia are effects of MDMA intoxication, not the nonspecific withdrawal syndrome of depressants.

educationalObjective: Nonspecific depressant withdrawal causes anxiety, tremor, seizures, and insomnia from rebound excitation after chronic sedative use.
